title: Problem Solving and Algorithms in Kasa
description: Five guided algorithm labs using core Kasa: tracing, searching, max-value scanning, sorting, and cost analysis. All lessons are text-first and do not change CMS video or transcript records.

units.title: Trace an algorithm step by step
units.goal: Break a problem into inputs, operations and outputs, then trace each step.
units.concept: An algorithm is a finite, clear set of instructions. A trace records how variables change; it is not guesswork.
units.source:
ma basket = [12, 8, 5]
ma total = 0
ma i = 0
bere_a i < tentɛn(basket)
    ma total = total + basket[i]
    ma i = i + 1
awiei
ka total
trace: Add 12, then 8, then 5 while moving to the next list position.
After index 2, i becomes 3; the loop condition is false and the total 25 is printed.
units.task: Predict the total for [12, 8, 5, 10] before running. Draw a table with one row per loop iteration.
acceptance: Records each change to total and i.
Explains why the loop stops without accessing an invalid index.
Keeps the computed total rather than hardcoding 35.
units.question: How many loop iterations run when the list contains three values?
units.answer: Three iterations. The valid indices are 0, 1 and 2.
units.complexity: One step per list item gives linear O(n) work.
units.mode: Core Kasa — runnable in the Academy lesson editor.

units.title: Find an item with linear search
units.goal: Search a list without assuming its values are sorted.
units.concept: Linear search inspects items in sequence until a match is found or the collection ends. A Boolean indicates whether we found a match.
units.source:
ma items = [14, 22, 9, 31]
ma wanted = 9
ma found = atoro
ma i = 0
bere_a i < tentɛn(items)
    sɛ items[i] == wanted a
        ma found = nokware
    awiei
    ma i = i + 1
awiei
ka found
trace: Start with found = atoro and wanted = 9.
Compare 14, then 22, then 9. At 9, set found to nokware.
This basic demonstration continues through the remaining item instead of stopping at the first match, then prints nokware.
units.task: Try wanted = 7 and predict the output. Modify the algorithm so it stops early with gyae once a match is found.
acceptance: Returns false when the list does not contain the target.
Tests both a first-position match and a missing match.
Explains that unsorted lists can require scanning all n values.
units.question: Does linear search require the list to be sorted?
units.answer: No. Linear search works on unsorted input.
units.complexity: In the worst case the search inspects n items, so time is O(n).
units.mode: Core Kasa — runnable in the Academy lesson editor.

units.title: Find the largest value safely
units.goal: Compute the maximum of a non-empty list while accounting for empty input.
units.concept: Initialize the maximum from the first real value, rather than incorrectly assuming all numbers are positive. The worked example assumes a non-empty list; add an explicit empty-list guard in your independent assignment.
units.source:
ma scores = [-8, -2, -15, -4]
ma largest = scores[0]
ma i = 1
bere_a i < tentɛn(scores)
    sɛ scores[i] > largest a
        ma largest = scores[i]
    awiei
    ma i = i + 1
awiei
ka largest
trace: Initialize largest to the first score, -8.
Compare -2 and replace largest; -15 is smaller, and so is -4.
The result is -2, which is the greatest value even though all numbers are negative.
units.task: Predict the result for [4, 16, 7, 12]. Add a check that avoids indexing position zero when the list is empty.
acceptance: Recognizes that scores[0] fails on an empty list.
Does not assume a fixed number of scores.
units.question: Why not initialize largest to 0?
units.answer: A list containing only negative values would incorrectly report 0, a value that is not in the input.
units.complexity: One pass through the list takes O(n) time and constant additional memory.
units.mode: Core Kasa — runnable in the Academy lesson editor.

units.title: Sort a list using comparisons
units.goal: Understand how repeated adjacent comparisons can order values.
units.concept: Bubble sort swaps adjacent out-of-order elements. This simple teaching algorithm is not the best general-purpose choice for large datasets.
units.source:
ma prices = [8, 3, 6, 1]
ma n = tentɛn(prices)
ma pass = 0
bere_a pass < n
    ma j = 0
    bere_a j + 1 < n
        sɛ prices[j] > prices[j + 1] a
            ma temp = prices[j]
            ma prices[j] = prices[j + 1]
            ma prices[j + 1] = temp
        awiei
        ma j = j + 1
    awiei
    ma pass = pass + 1
awiei
ka prices[0]
ka prices[1]
ka prices[2]
ka prices[3]
trace: First pass moves larger values toward the right by swapping adjacent pairs.
Further passes remove remaining inversions until values are ordered.
units.task: Change the initial list to [5, 2, 5, 1]. Predict the sorted output. Explain how duplicate values behave and how a no-swaps flag could avoid unnecessary passes. Change the four print positions only after changing list length.
acceptance: Explains the adjacent comparison and swap.
Demonstrates sorted output for duplicate values.
Identifies the redundant passes and the O(n²) worst-case cost.
units.question: Why does bubble sort scale poorly on large lists?
units.answer: It repeatedly compares pairs across multiple passes, doing quadratic O(n²) work in typical worst-case analysis.
units.complexity: Two nested passes give O(n²) time; in-place swaps use O(1) additional space.
units.mode: Core Kasa — runnable in the Academy lesson editor.

units.title: Compare algorithm costs
units.goal: Count iterations and explain why input size affects runtime.
units.concept: Big-O expresses how work grows with input size, not an exact runtime in seconds. Comparing one loop to nested loops makes that visible.
units.source:
ma n = 4
ma linear = 0
ma i = 0
bere_a i < n
    ma linear = linear + 1
    ma i = i + 1
awiei
ma pairs = 0
ma a = 0
bere_a a < n
    ma b = 0
    bere_a b < n
        ma pairs = pairs + 1
        ma b = b + 1
    awiei
    ma a = a + 1
awiei
ka linear
ka pairs
trace: The single loop increments linear once per item: 4 times.
The nested loops increment pairs four times for each of four outer iterations: 16 times.
For input size n, these counts grow as n and n × n.
units.task: Set n to 2 and then 8. Predict the two counts before running. Explain why doubling n quadruples the nested-loop count.
acceptance: Predicts n and n² counts accurately.
Distinguishes growth rate from exact wall-clock speed.
Recognizes the difference between a constant and an input-dependent loop bound.
units.question: If n doubles, what happens to n² operations?
units.answer: The count increases by a factor of four: (2n)² = 4n².
units.complexity: Single loop: O(n). Nested loops: O(n²).
units.mode: Core Kasa — runnable in the Academy lesson editor.
